transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Martin (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Veridian Eng Manager), Tom Becker (SRE), Alina Chen (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Product), Speaker 1 (contractor)

Summary:
Quick recap of last week's steady-state run, results from continuous batching adjustments, and proposed concurrency matrix to hit 95th percentile latency SLO while keeping cost within their target. Actionable tuning steps and benchmarking cadence agreed.

Topics:
- Continuous batching effects on tail latency
- Concurrency targets and per-GPU queueing strategy
- KV-cache warming and prefix cache hit-rate implications
- Fallbacks and burst capacity policy for spikes
- Next benchmark and ownership

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Sophie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we just wanted to run through the numbers from the last pilot run and then get alignment on tuning steps. Diego is gonna lead the tuning bits.
[00:00:18] Priya (Veridian): Thanks Sophie, yeah appreciate it. We've been watching the dashboards, see the throughput bump when you turned on continuous batching but also saw a few tail spikes that worried the product team.
[00:00:34] Diego (Redwood SE): Right, so the tradeoff we're trying to navigate is batching improves tokens per second but it can increase queuing at the front end which shows up as 95th/99th spikes, especially with our current concurrency of 8 workers per GPU. We dialed up the batch max to 64 last run which helped median latency but, um, the tail increased on some longer-context requests.
[00:01:05] Tom (SRE): I can jump in — we saw two windows around 03:14 and 03:35 UTC where the queue depth hit ~220, and the host CPU hit 85% so we had a brief backlog. That backlog manifested as 500ms extra wait before token generation actually started.
[00:01:26] Alina (ML Eng): Quick clarifying Q: when you say "batch max 64" is that global per-GPU or per-inference-worker? I think that was ambiguous in the config we ran.
[00:01:40] Diego (Redwood SE): Good call — that was global per-GPU in the runtime we used. We should probably switch to queue-aware per-worker caps for the next pass so it doesn't oversubscribe one host.
[00:01:55] Priya: Also how did KV cache warm-up look? There's a lot of repeated prefixes for our use-case and if cold misses cost us a lot then batching isn't helping.
[00:02:07] Diego: Cache hit rate was about 38% on average during peak, which is lower than expected; prefix lengths vary a lot. We recommended enabling sticky-key routing or prefix pinning to raise that.
[00:02:21] Samir (Product): Sticky-key routing meaning route similar customer sessions to the same GPU so the KV cache stays warm? That makes sense but does it cause hotspots?
[00:02:34] Diego: It can. The mitigation is to combine hashing with capacity-aware routing — i.e., prefer the sticky target but allow overflow to other GPUs when the target's queue exceeds a threshold.
[00:02:48] Speaker 1 (contractor): I flagged earlier that some requests have very long system prompts that inflate token counts unpredictably, that may be skewing the batching shapes.
[00:02:58] Sophie: Noted, we'll include prompt-length bucketing in the replay harness.
[00:03:08] Tom: On the networking side, we saw occasional serialization delays — protobuf marshalling on the client side was a bottleneck. We already have a fix queued up to stream protobuf frames which should shave 30-40ms.
[00:03:22] Alina: If we combine that with per-worker batch caps and sticky routing we should get both better cache hits and more predictable tail.
[00:03:34] Diego: Exactly. For the upcoming run I propose these concrete tuning changes: reduce global concurrency from 8 to 6, set per-worker batch_max to 32, add queue_threshold at 180 to trigger overflow, and enable prefix-pin for the top 20% of session keys.
[00:03:54] Priya: Can you justify the concurrency reduction? Won't that hurt throughput?
[00:03:59] Diego: Slight diagram: with high concurrency you reduce batching opportunities because each worker holds a slot, plus you increase lock contention for the KV store. By lowering concurrency we increase average batch size per worker which raises tokens/sec; on our sim it improved median throughput by 10% while lowering 95th latency by ~120ms. So throughput didn't lose, tails improved.
[00:04:28] Samir: Did you simulate the spike behavior? If we reduce concurrency, during sudden bursts will we see queuing that causes errors?
[00:04:35] Diego: We tested with a 5x spike and the overflow policy routed to a warm fallback pool (lower-capacity but higher concurrency) — that added about 20% cost for the spike but prevented errors. We'll send details.
[00:04:50] Tom: We need explicit throttling/ingress shaping on our side too, we can't simply rely on the runtime fallback; we'll add a leaky bucket limiter for the edge.
[00:04:59] Priya: On security/compliance: our SOC2 team asked about logs — did Redwood keep request-level logs with payloads?
[00:05:07] Sophie: No, by default we store traces and telemetry but not raw prompt text in hosted. For Private you can configure to keep logs or push to your SIEM. We have KMS integrations for encryption at rest and HSM options for private deployment.
[00:05:23] Alina: For the quantized variant we tried (int8), we saw an occasional hallucination pattern in structured outputs — is that expected?
[00:05:33] Diego: It's model-dependent; int8 can change some probabilities. In our tests differences were minor but if you have strict quality gating we can keep a fallback to a fp16 model for critical routing. That was in the rollout plan.
[00:05:48] Priya: Ok, quality is non-negotiable for some flows. We'll run a small eval suite on the quantized model and flag any regressions.
[00:05:58] Diego: Great. Another note — the runtime now supports batching timeouts and adaptive batching: if queue occupancy is low it waits up to X ms to form a batch. We tuned X to 20ms for your workload but we can try 10/30 to see latency/throughput tradeoffs.
[00:06:20] Sophie: We saw in your logs some requests that were consistently hitting the 100ms internal wait, probably because of the timeout choice.
[00:06:27] Tom: That's true — that 100ms timer was defaulted in our agent, we can lower it.
[00:06:31] Priya: Would lowering the agent's timeout cause more small batches and reduce overall efficiency?
[00:06:38] Diego: There's a sweet spot. With lower timeout you reduce tail for interactive requests but you sacrifice batching efficiency. Our recommendation is to set adaptive timeout by session type: interactive sessions get 10ms, background jobs get 40ms.
[00:06:56] Samir: Let's talk numbers — what's the expected cost delta if we keep the tuning vs revert? We need that for the CFO.
[00:07:04] Sophie: I'll send a cost delta sheet — rough number from our pilot sim was a 6-8% token-cost reduction due to better batching and a 15% compute cost delta during spikes when fallback pool is used. We'll quantify per-hour.
[00:07:19] Priya: That helps. One more ops question: for dedicated capacity, can we reserve burst capacity? Our compliance people want predictable budgets.
[00:07:30] Sophie: Yes, Redwood Dedicated supports reserved baseline and burst buckets; burst is billed at a premium but we can set hard caps and alerting.
[00:07:39] Alina: For the steady-state run you mentioned, can you share the replay harness and the exact config we used? We want to reproduce locally.
[00:07:46] Diego: Already prepping that. I'll upload a replay harness — it includes prompt bucketing, length profiles, and network delay simulation.
[00:07:54] Speaker 1: I did a quick comparison vs Anthropic on a similar job — they had lower median but worse 99th, seems consistent with what you're showing.
[00:08:05] Diego: Competitor notes are useful — our focus is stable tails.
[00:08:10] Priya: Ok let's lock the next benchmark: Diego + Tom to run a coordinated 12-hr steady-state with the proposed config, log traces, and then we'll all review.
[00:08:20] Sophie: Proposed schedule?
[00:08:22] Tom: Can do Monday 2026-11-23 10:00 PST for the benchmark kickoff.
[00:08:28] Sophie: Great. Diego, can you put the config in the repo and Samir will trigger the run?
[00:08:33] Diego: Yep. I'll tag the repo and include a small harness.
[00:08:38] Alina: One tiny thing — can we add a health-check endpoint that returns current batch sizes on that GPU? That would help real-time ops.
[00:08:46] Diego: We have an endpoint for that; we'll enable it and show you the schema.
[00:08:52] Priya: Anything else on fallbacks?
[00:08:55] Sophie: We should document the fallback cost and expected latency. I'll add that to the pricing note.
[00:08:59] Samir: Also include the RBAC rules for who can flip the fallback on/off in the console.
[00:09:06] Sophie: Good call.
[00:09:08] (discussion moves to clarifying small config flags and timeline)
[00:18:32] (Diego walks through a short sharing of the sample config and shows simulated graphs — transcription is rough here, audio glitch 00:18:50)
[00:20:10] Diego: So the recommended matrix: concurrency 6, batch_max 32, batch_timeout adaptive (10ms interactive / 40ms batch), queue_threshold 180, overflow target to warm-fallback pool, prefix-pin top 20%.
[00:21:02] Priya: We'll try that. Can you add a second line that favors lower latency (concurrency 8, batch_max 24) so we can compare?
[00:21:12] Diego: Sure — I'll include both profiles and a small cost-latency chart.
[00:21:20] Tom: I'll export the ingress metrics and attach them.
[00:21:26] Alina: After the 12-hr run we'll do a quality regression on the top 50 prompt sets.
[00:21:33] Sophie: Perfect.
[00:21:35] (wrap up, final recaps)
[00:22:10] Sophie: Recap: Diego uploads config and harness by 2026-11-21, Sophie shares pricing delta and fallback docs by 2026-11-21, Tom provides ingress/export metrics by 2026-11-20, Veridian runs 12-hr steady-state on 2026-11-23 and shares traces, Alina runs quality eval by 2026-11-24.
[00:22:30] Priya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:22:34] Samir: Thanks, we'll follow up in Slack with any blockers.
[00:22:36] Diego: Thanks all.
[00:22:40] (meeting ends)
